outcome: Nothing since 26 January 2024 settles the Williamson conjecture as Wikipedia words it (Williamson matrices of every order n), which was already false from 1993 at order 35. The one post-2024 claim of new Williamson matrices is a 2025 Missouri dissertation for orders 72 to 124 (not readable to me), whose novelty is doubtful against 2018 to 2020 doubling results. The 2026 preprints I found concern neighbouring objects (near-Williamson, complex, quaternionic and Goethals-Seidel matrices). An AI-credited Hadamard matrix of order 668 (announced 12 August 2026, credited to Claude) is a Hadamard-parent event, and no source I could open ties it to Williamson matrices.
problem_asks: (a) For every positive integer n, whether Williamson matrices of order n exist, where a Williamson matrix of order n is a quadruple A, B, C, D of symmetric circulant n x n matrices with entries +1 or -1 and A^2 + B^2 + C^2 + D^2 = 4nI. This is the conjecture as the Wikipedia article 'Williamson conjecture' states it ('for all positive integers' n). (b) The use the bullet names: Williamson's 1944 block construction turns four Williamson matrices of order n into a Hadamard matrix of order 4n (a theorem, not in question). The bullet's 'can be used to construct Hadamard matrices' is read as the hope that this gives Hadamard matrices in every order 4n, which Wikipedia says was once hoped to prove the Hadamard conjecture. (c) As a sub-question of (a): existence of Williamson matrices in every even order. (d) As a sub-question of (a): existence in every odd order. The sources I read settle odd n < 65 (they exist except n = 35, 47, 53, 59) and leave odd n >= 65 open; 65 and 67 are the named open cases in what I read. The bullet names no particular order, so (a) is decided by any single failing order, and (c) and (d) are not touched by that failure.

events.what_happened: Turyn's construction, as reported second-hand (in a search summary of the Bright, Kotsireas, Ganesh 2018 paper and a Waterloo report): from a Williamson matrix of odd order n, Williamson matrices of orders 2^k * n for k = 1, 2, 3, 4. One source dates it 1970, another 1972. I did not locate or open the original.
events.revisions: Year disputed between 1970 and 1972 in secondary sources.
events.delivers: As reported: Williamson matrices of orders 2^k * n (k = 1 to 4) from each odd-order Williamson matrix of order n. Hypotheses not read. The route cannot reach 2^k * n for odd n with no Williamson matrix, so 70 = 2 * 35, 94 = 2 * 47, 106 = 2 * 53 and 118 = 2 * 59 are not reached by it.
events.remains: Every order 2^k * m with m odd and having no Williamson matrix (35, 47, 53, 59 and any other unresolved odd order), and every even order not of the form 2^k * (odd).
events.directly_checkable: Each output matrix can be checked by computing the four squares and summing; no specific matrix is named in the sources I read.
events.doubts: Second-hand only. The 1974 Seberry-Wallis gap list (event 2) still lists 76 = 4 * 19 as open, which is hard to square with a 1970 or 1972 construction giving 76 from order 19. I found no source resolving this.
events.direction: Positive: a route to even orders from odd-order Williamson matrices. It is blocked where the odd order has no Williamson matrix, as Bright, Kotsireas and Ganesh note for order 70.

events.what_happened: C. Bright, I. Kotsireas and V. Ganesh, 'A SAT+CAS method for enumerating Williamson matrices of even order', AAAI-18 (Thirty-Second AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence, 2018), DOI 10.1609/aaai.v32i1.12203. The abstract says Williamson matrices exist for every even order n < 65 and do not exist at orders 35, 47, 53 and 59, and that 'prior to our work, Williamson matrices had only been enumerated for odd orders n < 60'. The companion arXiv:1804.01172 (v1 3 April 2018, later than the AAAI paper; v2 14 May 2019, accepted in the Journal of Symbolic Computation) extends the even-order enumeration to all even orders up to and including 70, builds 8-Williamson matrices in all odd orders up to 35, and finds one previously unknown set of Williamson matrices of order 63 (odd). It says Turyn's construction cannot give order 70, so 70 was settled by direct search.
events.revisions: arXiv:1804.01172 v1 3 April 2018; v2 14 May 2019; Journal of Symbolic Computation publication (ScienceDirect S0747717119300902, year not read).
events.delivers: Williamson matrices exist for every even order n <= 70 (the arXiv scope; the AAAI scope is n < 65). Order 70 is settled by direct search. A new odd-order set for 63. Odd order 8-Williamson matrices up to 35 (not Williamson). The even-order result is a finite census of instances of the universal claim that every even order works. Under the scope test in DEEP_DIVE section 2.1 that is an instance count, so the judging pass should decide whether it moves the problem's quantity.
events.remains: Even orders above 70 (in part covered by doubling; in part open, e.g. 94 = 2 * 47, 106 = 2 * 53, 118 = 2 * 59), and odd orders 65 and above (open in what I read).

events.what_happened: Santiago Barrera Acevedo and Heiko Dietrich, 'New infinite families of Williamson Hadamard matrices', Australasian Journal of Combinatorics 73(1) (2019) 207-219. Abstract: there are Williamson matrices of order 4a(q+1) for each a in {1, 11, 17, 23, 29, 33, 39, 43}; of order 2(q+1)(r+1) when gcd(q+1, r+1) = 2; and of order 2^b(q+1) for b in {2,...,7}, with q and r prime powers congruent to 1 mod 4. The abstract also gives Williamson-type matrices with circulant blocks of order 2^c(q+1) for c in {5, 6}. The proofs use perfect quaternionic sequences and relative difference sets. Opened.

events.remains: Every even order outside the families (e.g. 94, 106, 118), and all odd orders.

events.what_happened: Raymond Nguyen (advisor Stephen Montgomery-Smith), 'Optimal frames, the Hadamard conjecture, and Williamson matrices of order an odd multiple of 4', University of Missouri doctoral dissertation, 2025 (MOspace item fe169df1-fa80-4b45-b119-264db3a2aa05). Per a search-result abstract summary (the PDF and item page returned HTTP 403, and the handle returned connection refused): a new framework for finding Williamson matrices of order a multiple of 4; examples at orders 72, 76, 84, 92, 100, 108, 116 and 124, with 92 and 116 'constructed without using Williamson matrices of lower order'; the conjecture that Williamson matrices exist in every order that is an odd multiple of 4, which would give Hadamard matrices in every odd multiple of 16. The frame-theory half concerns Cahill-Casazza problems and is not this bullet.
events.delivers: Claimed examples of Williamson matrices at the eight orders 72, 76, 84, 92, 100, 108, 116 and 124. Each of these is 2^t times an odd order that has Williamson matrices (9, 19, 21, 23, 25, 27, 29, 31), so the 2019/2020 sequence result (event 11) and the 2018 doubling (event 8) cover them, if they carry over to matrices. The thesis's novelty claim is therefore doubtful at least for 76 (named as open in 1974) and for the existence of the other orders, and may only concern construction method. The conjecture for all odd multiples of 4 is a conjecture only.
events.remains: The conjecture for all orders 4 * (odd), which is not settled by these examples. This includes 140 = 4 * 35, 188 = 4 * 47, 212 = 4 * 53 and 236 = 4 * 59, where the odd part has no Williamson matrix. Even orders not of the form 4 * odd (e.g. 94 = 2 * 47, 106, 118) are not addressed.

events.what_happened: Hadi Kharaghani, Ali Mohammadian and Behruz Tayfeh-Rezaie (plus Vlad Zaitsev in a later version), 'A search for Hadamard matrices of near-Williamson type', arXiv:2605.08661. Near-Williamson matrices: A circulant, B, C, D symmetric circulant, with AA^T + BB^T + CC^T + DD^T = 4nI. Version 1 (9 May 2026; three authors on the abstract page) says: a computer search classifies all inequivalent near-Williamson matrices for odd orders at most 35; they exist for all odd orders up to 63; first known quaternary Hadamard matrix of order 118. A later version (arXiv listing 6 September 2026) is read in two different ways. The HTML page gives four authors, classification to odd order 47, existence 'for every odd order n <= 69', and quaternary Hadamard orders 94, 118, 130, 134, 206 and 266. The abstract page for v2 gives the earlier numbers (35, 63, 118) with three authors. The two readings conflict and I could not resolve this.

events.doubts: Version conflict as above. Computer-search results come from two programs run on two computers (per the HTML page). Odd orders 65 and 67 are mentioned in a search summary as near-Williamson examples; I did not read that in the paper and do not rely on it.

disputes.summary: arXiv:2605.08661: the abstract page and the HTML page disagree about the later version. Abstract page: three authors, classification to odd order 35, existence to 63, first quaternary Hadamard matrix of order 118. HTML page: four authors (adding Vlad Zaitsev), classification to 47, existence to 69, quaternary orders 94, 118, 130, 134, 206, 266. This is a version conflict, not a priority dispute. The PDF would settle it.

Order 76 and the other orders in the Nguyen thesis (72 to 124). The thesis claims examples there, and calls 76 an order open since 1974. The 2018 doubling construction (arXiv:1803.01480), the 2019/2020 sequence result (arXiv:1905.00267) and Turyn's construction (as reported, 1970 or 1972) would give 76 = 4 * 19 from a Williamson matrix of order 19 if they carry over to matrices. No source I read resolves which result came first, or whether the older results apply to matrices.

Order 668 (parent event, not Williamson): Epoch lists it as 'Solved (human + AI)' and 'First solved with: Claude (internal Anthropic model)', and says it is provisionally marked as solved by AI and will be revised if humans contributed significantly. Wikipedia lists it as an AI discovery. The authors' post credits a weekend with several collaborators and 'of course claude'. No authors' account of what each contributed was found.

summary: The Wikipedia conjecture (Williamson matrices exist for all positive integers n) was refuted in 1993 by Djokovic's exhaustive search at order 35, and 2008 added 47, 53 and 59 (Holzmann, Kharaghani, Tayfeh-Rezaie). By 2018 the even orders up to 70 were enumerated (Bright, Kotsireas, Ganesh), with 70 settled by search because Turyn's route needs a Williamson matrix of order 35. The 2018 doubling (arXiv:1803.01480) and the 2019/2020 sequence result (arXiv:1905.00267; IEEE 2020) give even orders 2^t times an odd order with Williamson matrices; the sequence result is stated for sequences and I took the matrix consequence as an inference. Within the window, the only post-2024 Williamson-matrix existence claim I found is Nguyen's 2025 Missouri dissertation (orders 72 to 124, plus a conjecture for all odd multiples of 4). I could not open the thesis (HTTP 403 and connection refused), and every order it names is 2^t times an odd order that the 2018 to 2020 results already cover, so the thesis is at most new in method. The 2026 preprints (Bennett et al. on non-symmetric Williamson-type matrices up to order 21; Szollosi's complex Hadamard matrix of order 94 from order-47 circulants; Kharaghani et al.'s near-Williamson matrices, whose version scope conflicts between the two readings I got) concern neighbouring objects and do not settle Williamson existence. The Williamson, Yacobi, Zinn-Justin transformer paper is about Hadamard matrices of another family, and its first author is not the Williamson of the matrices. The Hadamard-parent event with AI is Alpoge's August 2026 announcement of order 668 and eleven other orders, credited to Claude (internal Anthropic model) by Epoch; I could not open the authors' posts or a paper, and no source I read says Williamson matrices were used. Close calls: (i) whether the even-order census to 70 and the sequence families count as moving the even-order question, or only as instance counts of a universal claim; (ii) whether the thesis's claims are new given the 2018 to 2020 results; (iii) whether the Alpoge construction used Williamson-type blocks. Remaining open after the window, on what I read: even orders such as 94 (2 * 47), 106, 118, and 4 * (35, 47, 53, 59) = 140, 188, 212, 236, and odd orders 65 and above (other than 69, which Bright et al. list as having one set). No source I found settles 94.
competing_reading: (1) The bullet can be read as the even-order existence question, which is open and has a 2025 claim behind it, so the Nguyen thesis would be a real event and the record would look like a partial advance. (2) Read as Wikipedia's conjecture (all orders), it has been false since 1993, and the record is a settled negative with nothing new in the window. (3) Read as a Hadamard question, the 668 result is an AI-credited Hadamard advance, but it is only relevant to this bullet if its construction used Williamson-type blocks, which nothing I read establishes.
what_would_settle_it: (a) The Nguyen thesis PDF: whether it cites the 2018 doubling and the 2019/2020 sequence results, and whether it claims novelty of existence or only of construction for 72 to 124. (b) The 1905.00267 IEEE paper's section on matrices, to confirm the matrix consequence. (c) The arXiv:2605.08661 PDF, to resolve which version has which scope and authors. (d) Alpoge's posts or any technical report on the 668 construction: whether it uses Williamson matrices, Turyn-type sequences or base sequences. (e) A list of even orders above 70 with no Williamson matrix, from any source after 2020, to decide whether 94 is settled. (f) The Turyn primary source (1970 or 1972) and the 1974 Seberry-Wallis list, to settle whether 76 was open when the doubling results were proved.

judgement.why: The statement asks for Williamson matrices of every order. Djokovic's 1993 exhaustive search showed none exist at order 35, which answers the whole question in the negative. A journal published it and it was later re-checked independently by SAT, so it counts as digested. That event is before the snapshot. Later results either settle families of orders (case) or check single or finitely many orders (instances). Every event after the snapshot is about a different object — near-Williamson, complex, quaternionic, Goethals-Seidel or modular matrices, or Hadamard matrices of order 668 — so each is a variant. The exception is Nguyen's thesis, which claims finitely many orders that earlier results already appear to cover, so it is instances. The AI roles on the two Hadamard events have no effect because both are variants.
judgement.doubts: The AI roles for the transformer paper and the order-668 announcement rest on thin quotes. For order 668, 'of course claude' does not say what Claude produced. Djokovic's object role is left null: the result is a non-existence proof, not an exhibited object, although order 35 does act as the counterexample.
